title: Data vs Hype: How Orgs Actually Win with AI - The Pragmatic Summit
summary: DX's industry benchmarks (~92% adoption, ~4 hours/week saved, ~27% AI-authored code, faster onboarding) and the argument that AI amplifies existing org strengths and weaknesses and needs organizational change.

assertions.quote: sitting around 92.6 of developers are using an AI coding assistant at least once a month
We're sitting around 4.08 uh self-reported hours saved due to AI tool usage per week per developer.
we're at about 26.9% industrywide for all of these developers
Uh AI is fantastic for onboarding.

verdicts.note: Vendor telemetry shows time-to-10th-PR falling alongside AI adoption, but that is correlational and not independently verified.

METR RCT: developers were slowed less on issues with low prior exposure and high reference needs, and said AI helps most with unfamiliar code (e.g. Git hooks, finding unknown helpers). Onboarding time itself was not measured, and the main result was a 19% slowdown for familiar experts.

At Microsoft, recent hires (below-median tenure) raised Copilot-assisted output by 27-39% vs 8-13% for long-tenure staff. That is consistent with AI helping newer developers, but onboarding time itself was not measured and the differences are not significant.

Eight participants new to Java/Spring said AI was valuable for getting up to speed, and some used it only for onboarding. The evidence is qualitative self-report from a non-randomized phase, not a measured onboarding time.

assertions.quote: AI is an accelerator. It's a multiplier and it is moving organizations off in different directions.
high adoption but actually low transformation
a developer sitting at their desk there is a very very low ceiling of productivity gain.
just giving all of your developers licenses and hoping for the best. It does not work.
Come to find out, in fact, these are the things that make AI really successful.
